pages.title: About
pages.content:
About

A small agency for two-room meetings

Founded in Rotterdam in 2011, Koe Interpreters coordinates conference interpreting teams for bilingual and multilingual meetings across Europe.

Founded in Rotterdam, 2011 ·

Founded 2011 in Rotterdam

Founded in 2011 at Havenkade 14 in Rotterdam, Koe Interpreters was established to provide dependable conference interpreting for high-stakes business and institutional proceedings. From the outset, we focused on five working languages: English, Traditional Chinese (Mandarin), Japanese, French, and German. Rotterdam's international port and European transport links gave us immediate access to industrial, maritime, and diplomatic gatherings. Over the years, our operational model has remained steady. We manage every assignment from our central request desk, maintaining direct communication between event organizers and our practicing conference interpreters. We do not operate as an anonymous directory or general translation broker. Every meeting we accept is handled with personal accountability, rigorous linguistic preparation, and professional decorum.

Why we only staff booths we can brief

Interpreting is only as solid as the preparatory work completed before the microphone turns on. We only accept assignments where our interpreters can receive meeting documentation in advance and conduct a focused briefing call with the speakers or organizers. When a brief arrives, we verify that background slide decks, agendas, participant lists, and draft resolutions will be shared at least five working days ahead of the event. This preparation allows each interpreter to build a verified glossary of specialized terminology, align on specific pronunciation of proper names, and anticipate the pace of proceedings. If an organizer cannot provide basic briefing access or context, we decline the assignment rather than compromise the clarity of the room.

How the roster of 38 is kept small enough to know

Our working roster is strictly limited to 38 accredited conference interpreters across our five languages. Rather than maintaining a database of hundreds of unvetted freelance contacts, we work exclusively with colleagues whose booth stamina, voice control, and ethical standards we know intimately. Every interpreter on our roster is accustomed to our strict booth discipline: two interpreters per language pair, alternating turns precisely every 30 minutes to maintain sharp cognitive focus. Founder Ines Okonkwo-Bauer and our booth leads personally assign each team member based on industry domain, technical complexity, and booth compatibility. This deliberate scale ensures that when we confirm a team, we know exactly who will be speaking on your behalf.

The people you will meet

When you contact our desk and run an event with Koe Interpreters, you will work directly with our key practitioners and coordinators: Ines Okonkwo-Bauer: founder and chief interpreter, working across EN ⇄ DE ⇄ FR. Kenji Haraguchi: booth lead for EN ⇄ JA assignments. Mei-Lin Chou: specialist interpreter for EN ⇄ ZH press conferences and trade delegations. Camille Dufresne: covering FR ⇄ EN and FR ⇄ DE for policy round tables. Tobias Lindqvist: covering DE ⇄ EN for complex engineering reviews and medical briefs. Aiko Brennan: handling JA ⇄ EN and managing relay booths for three-language days. Samuel Adeyemi: head of our request desk and scheduling coordination at Havenkade 14.

Request desk and scheduling

From 2011 to today

Since our founding in 2011, Koe Interpreters has supported hundreds of board meetings, technical symposia, and bilateral trade talks. While conference presentation technology and event formats continue to evolve, the essential challenge of simultaneous interpretation remains unchanged. It demands unwavering concentration, deep subject familiarity, and a steady human voice that bridges two languages without drawing attention to itself. Operating from our Rotterdam office, we continue to uphold these foundational standards for every client, ensuring that discussions across English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, French, and German proceed as naturally as conversations held in a single tongue.

pages.title: Briefs
pages.content:
Briefs

Which meetings a brief suits

We organize conference interpreting teams across nine established language configurations and four primary meeting families.

Nine ways to staff a booth ·

Language pairs and booth configurations

We support nine specific language configurations across our five working languages.

EN ⇄ JA

Board and investor meetings

EN ⇄ ZH

Press conferences and trade delegations

EN ⇄ FR

Policy round tables and governance discussions

EN ⇄ DE

Engineering reviews and works councils

FR ⇄ DE

Cross-border plenaries and bilateral negotiations

JA ⇄ ZH

Factory visits and supplier days

JA → FR via EN

Relay booth configuration for three-language days

ZH → DE via EN

Relay booth configuration for medical symposia

Consecutive

Small executive rooms, site visits, and diplomatic dinners

Each simultaneous pair is staffed by two interpreters in an ISO-compliant soundproof booth, switching every 30 minutes.

Board and investor meetings

Executive board discussions and investor presentations require absolute precision, confidentiality, and calm pacing under pressure. When submitting a brief for a board or shareholder meeting, organizers should provide the agenda, quarterly financial statements, strategic slide decks, and participant profiles. We typically assign a two-interpreter booth for bilateral sessions, such as our frequent EN ⇄ JA assignments for multinational enterprises. Our interpreters sign binding non-disclosure agreements and familiarize themselves with your corporate metrics, governance terminology, and executive speaking habits well before the opening gavel. For an example of how we handle executive proceedings, read our story regarding two days with a shipping group board.

Read the story: two days, one board →

Press conferences and trade delegations

Press briefings and international trade delegations move quickly, featuring rapid announcements, unplanned questions from journalists, and varied regional accents. A brief for these events must specify expected attendance, audio-visual broadcast plans, speaker lists, and press release drafts under embargo. We deploy two interpreters per language pair, commonly EN ⇄ ZH, to handle the rapid exchange of information without hesitation. Our teams excel at maintaining composure during live question-and-answer periods where clarity is paramount. Organizers can read our documented case detailing how we assembled a full Chinese interpreting team for a consumer-electronics maker on just 48 hours' notice.

Read the story: a press conference at 48 hours' notice →

Technical and medical symposia

Scientific conferences and technical congresses demand rigorous terminology management and seamless multilateral coordination. Briefs for symposia must include speaker abstracts, clinical or technical papers, presentation slides, and specialized acronym reference lists. When proceedings cover three languages, such as Japanese, German, and English, we establish two booths operating via English relay. Tobias Lindqvist and Aiko Brennan frequently lead these complex setups, ensuring terminology remains perfectly unified across both booths. Review our published case study describing how a medical-device association conducted a multi-day conference across three languages through one central English relay booth.

Read the story: three languages through one relay →

Site visits and dinners

Informal meeting environments, factory floor tours, audit inspections, and executive dinners require flexible, unobtrusive interpretation. Rather than soundproof booths, these assignments utilize consecutive interpreting or portable whisper equipment. Your brief should outline the walking itinerary, background ambient noise levels, expected dining speeches, and overall group size. We assign seasoned consecutive specialists who take concise shorthand notes beside the principal speaker, reproducing statements with complete factual fidelity. This format allows visiting delegations to inspect manufacturing facilities or build relationships over dinner while communicating effortlessly with local management.

Read: consecutive notes, explained →

pages.title: Meeting day
pages.content:
Meeting day

One booth, two voices

On the day of your conference, our interpreters follow a disciplined schedule and established booth protocol so the delivery stays clear and continuous.

Turns every 30 minutes ·

The schedule from arrival to closing

Every conference day follows five coordinated milestones on our operational schedule.

07:45

Our interpreter team arrives on site at your venue to conduct a complete glossary read-through and review any late agenda revisions.

08:15

We conduct a thorough 30-minute sound check alongside the AV technician, testing console levels, headsets, and microphone feeds.

09:00

The opening plenary begins, with interpreters alternating turns every 30 minutes to maintain peak cognitive acuity.

12:30

The team takes lunch while exchanging handover notes between booths regarding morning terminology.

17:30

Proceedings conclude, and the chief interpreter files final glossary updates.

Team composition and booth rules

Our team composition follows professional standards designed to protect acoustic quality and listener comprehension.

One pair, one booth

For any single language pair, we staff one soundproof booth with exactly two conference interpreters. Turns change every 30 minutes, as simultaneous interpretation causes rapid mental fatigue that compromises accuracy after prolonged stretches.

Three languages, two booths

When an event requires three languages, such as Japanese, German, and French, we establish two separate booths that coordinate through an English relay.

Long days, a third interpreter

For demanding conference days exceeding 6.5 hours of active meeting time, we assign a third interpreter per booth to maintain sustainable rotations throughout extended evening sessions.

Acoustic standards and equipment requirements

Clear interpretation relies on clean audio feeds and proper acoustic containment. We work exclusively with soundproof booths built to international ISO standards, ensuring adequate air circulation, unobstructed sightlines to the stage, and total acoustic separation from the main hall. Each booth is furnished with two professional interpreter consoles, high-fidelity headsets, and dedicated cough switches. For delegates, we provide clean, multi-channel wireless receivers and lightweight earpieces distributed at registration. An experienced audiovisual technician remains on site throughout the entire day to monitor channel frequencies, adjust input volumes, and resolve any technical irregularities before they reach the audience.

How do booth handovers work during live speeches?

A question clients often ask is how interpreters switch places without interrupting the flow of the speaker. In our booths, handovers occur silently every 30 minutes. The active interpreter continues speaking into the console microphone while the incoming colleague listens on their secondary headset. At an appropriate sentence boundary, the active interpreter signals with two fingers, touches the mute or channel transfer control, and the colleague immediately takes over the transmission. This seamless switch ensures that delegates listening on receivers hear a steady, uninterrupted stream of interpretation without sudden pauses, volume spikes, or lost thoughts.

pages.title: Rates
pages.content:
Rates

Rates, per interpreter

We publish transparent, fixed rates for our conference interpreting services, booth equipment, and preparatory work across all five languages.

EUR, excluding VAT and travel ·

Fee schedule per interpreter and service

Our published rates apply uniformly to English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, French, and German assignments.

Prices in EUR, excluding VAT and travel. Same rates in every language.

Worked pricing example

To understand how our fees are calculated for a standard corporate event, consider a typical one-day bilingual board meeting requiring English and Japanese interpretation. For this assignment, the team comprises two simultaneous interpreters working in a single booth. Each interpreter is billed at the full-day rate of €1,180, plus the mandatory preparation and briefing fee of €240. The calculation is: 2 interpreters × €1,180 + 2 × €240 preparation = €2,840. If your venue does not possess built-in ISO facilities, booth and receiver hire with a technician can be added for €1,450 per day, resulting in a clear, predictable budget.

A one-day bilingual board meeting: 2 interpreters × €1,180 + 2 × €240 preparation = €2,840.

Our three core operating commitments

Every booking with Koe Interpreters is underpinned by three foundational operating rules.

Two interpreters per booth

We never allow a single interpreter to work a simultaneous booth alone, safeguarding linguistic accuracy and cognitive stamina.

Strict 30-minute turns

Interpreters alternate speaking duties every half hour, ensuring steady delivery and continuous attention throughout the day.

One business day reply

Every brief submitted to our Rotterdam desk receives a detailed response and binding fixed quote within one business day, allowing you to finalize your event planning without administrative delays.

What are your cancellation and travel policies?

We recognize that conference schedules can shift due to external circumstances. Our cancellation policy is simple and fair: cancellations made more than 14 days before the scheduled event date incur no fee. Cancellations made between 7 and 14 days before the event are billed at 50% of the total quote. Cancellations made fewer than 7 days prior to opening are billed in full, at the whole quoted amount. Travel, lodging, and daily subsistence expenses for assignments outside the greater Rotterdam area are charged at direct cost without markup, and will be estimated clearly in your initial quote.

Request a team →

pages.title: Request a team
pages.content:
Request a team

Send us the brief

To book an interpreting team or receive a formal quote, submit your meeting brief to our Rotterdam desk.

We reply in one business day ·

Information to include in your brief

To provide an accurate quote and match your event with the appropriate specialists, please include the following six details in your initial email.

  1. Date and times. Scheduled start, adjournment, and required rehearsal or sound-check times.
  2. Venue or platform. Physical address and room name, or the virtual conferencing platform.
  3. Languages. Specific language pairs required across English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, French, or German.
  4. Agenda and documents. A preliminary schedule, subject overview, or presentation slide decks.
  5. Audience size. Estimated delegate count and number of receivers required.
  6. Contact person. Lead organizer name, telephone number, and billing address.
Email the brief →

Desk hours and contact channels

Our request desk is located at Havenkade 14, 3011 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands. Desk staff are on duty Monday to Friday, 08:30–18:00 CET. All initial inquiries, schedules, and document packages should be emailed directly to requests@koe-interpreters.example. We reply to every email brief within one business day with team availability and a binding quote. If you have an urgent inquiry for a meeting taking place within the next 72 hours, please contact our emergency line directly at +31 10 555 0140 for immediate assistance from our scheduling coordinator Samuel Adeyemi.

What happens next

Once you submit your initial brief, our coordination process follows three structured stages.

01

Within one business day of receiving your brief, our desk confirms interpreter availability and issues a binding, fixed-fee quote.

02

Meeting documents and slide presentations must be delivered five working days prior to the conference. We conduct a 20-minute briefing call with your team and distribute our compiled terminology glossary two days before the event.

03

On the meeting day, our interpreters arrive 75 minutes prior to the opening plenary for technical sound checks, and file completed glossary notes within two business days following adjournment.

How far in advance should we submit a brief?

We recommend submitting your brief four to eight weeks prior to your event date, particularly for multilingual configurations or peak spring and autumn conference seasons. However, we routinely accommodate shorter planning horizons when our roster permits. For assignments booked on short notice, our minimum requirement is receiving background presentation decks at least 48 hours before opening so our interpreters can complete essential terminology checks. If your event takes place in less than 72 hours, call our urgent desk line at +31 10 555 0140 to verify immediate interpreter availability.

Early access

The online brief, spring 2027

In spring 2027, Koe Interpreters will introduce a streamlined online brief tool to simplify conference quoting and document delivery.

Opens in spring 2027 ·

The online brief, launching spring 2027

The online brief is our upcoming digital submission platform designed to make booking conference interpreting teams faster, clearer, and more organized. Launching in spring 2027, this structured tool will allow meeting organizers, corporate event planners, and venue directors to configure their requirements in a few intuitive steps. Instead of exchanging fragmented email attachments, you can upload conference agendas, presentation slide decks, and specialized reference glossaries directly into a secure portal that routes materials straight to your assigned booth team. The system eliminates administrative delays and ensures every interpreter receives briefing documentation in an organized, timely manner.

Three functions of the online brief platform

When the platform opens in spring 2027, it will deliver three core operational capabilities.

Upload agenda and slides

You can drag and drop draft agendas, speaker lists, presentation decks, and technical background papers into a centralized, encrypted repository.

Pick languages and room plan

Select your required language pairs across English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, French, and German, and specify whether your room setup requires physical booths, relay channels, or consecutive seating.

Get a fixed quote in one business day

The portal calculates precise team requirements and generates a binding quote within one business day.

How to register for early access

We invite regular meeting planners, institutional secretaries, and event producers to participate in our early access release ahead of the public launch in spring 2027. Early participants will receive priority booking windows, dedicated onboarding support from desk coordinator Samuel Adeyemi, and direct opportunities to provide feedback on feature workflows. To reserve your place on the list, send an email to early@koe-interpreters.example with the subject line Early access. We do not distribute marketing newsletters or share your contact information with external parties; we will contact you solely with system onboarding instructions.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Privacy

How we handle your brief

Confidential by default ·

Data collection and conference materials

Koe Interpreters, located at Havenkade 14, 3011 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands, acts as the data controller for personal and corporate information provided through our request desk. When you submit a meeting brief, we collect organizer contact details, corporate billing information, venue logistics, and briefing documentation including agendas, speaker rosters, and presentation slide decks. We process this information exclusively to evaluate team availability, generate binding fee quotes, and prepare our conference interpreters for their assignments. We never sell, rent, or distribute client contact details or proprietary meeting materials to commercial third parties or external marketing networks.

Confidentiality and document retention

Due to the sensitive commercial, diplomatic, and legal nature of the proceedings we interpret, all briefing presentations, draft speeches, and corporate glossaries are treated with strict professional confidentiality. Our 38 accredited roster interpreters and administrative staff are bound by non-disclosure agreements. Digital briefing files are stored in access-restricted repositories accessible only to the interpreters assigned to your specific meeting. Following the conclusion of your event and the completion of post-meeting glossary filing within two business days, client working documents are permanently archived or deleted in accordance with our data retention schedule and European legal standards.

What rights do you have regarding your data?

Under European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) standards, organizers and meeting participants have the right to request access to the personal data we hold, request corrections to inaccurate records, or demand the deletion of non-essential contact information. If you wish to review the information stored by our desk, update your corporate billing details, or ask questions regarding our document disposal protocols, please contact our administrative desk at requests@koe-interpreters.example or by postal mail at Havenkade 14, 3011 AB Rotterdam. We respond to all formal privacy requests within one business day.

pages.title: Terms
pages.content:
Terms

Terms of engagement

Valid from 1 January 2027 ·

Rates validity and booking confirmation

The fee schedule published by Koe Interpreters is valid for all meetings booked from 1 January 2027 onward. All fees are quoted in EUR (€) and exclude value-added tax (VAT) and direct travel costs. A booking is formally confirmed when the client approves our written quote issued from Havenkade 14 in Rotterdam. Our standard pricing covers simultaneous full-day assignments up to 6.5 hours at €1,180 per interpreter, half-day sessions up to 3.5 hours at €720 per interpreter, and consecutive full days at €980 per interpreter. Preparation and briefing is charged at €240 per interpreter per meeting, and overtime is billed at €140 per interpreter for each started 30 minutes.

Cancellation schedule and terms

Because conference interpreters are booked exclusively and must decline other professional engagements for reserved dates, cancellations are subject to our established schedule: Cancellations received in writing more than 14 days prior to the first scheduled meeting day incur no cancellation fee. Cancellations received between 7 and 14 days prior to the event date are charged at 50% of the total confirmed quote. Cancellations received fewer than 7 days prior to the event date are charged the full confirmed quote. Any pre-booked non-refundable travel or lodging expenses incurred prior to cancellation remain payable by the client.

Working conditions and booth regulations

To safeguard the cognitive health of our interpreters and keep the rendition accurate for delegates, all bookings must respect our established booth regulations. For simultaneous interpreting, each language pair requires one ISO-compliant booth staffed by two qualified interpreters. Working turns must alternate every 30 minutes. For meetings where continuous active sessions exceed 6.5 hours, a third interpreter must be added to the booth roster. Clients must provide complete draft agendas and background presentation materials at least five working days before the meeting to enable proper preparation. Failure to provide adequate acoustic conditions or timely briefing documentation may result in team withdrawal.

posts.title: What the sound check is for
posts.excerpt: A rigorous thirty-minute sound check before the opening plenary protects both interpreter comprehension and audience listening comfort throughout the conference day.
posts.content:
At 08:15 on every conference morning, forty-five minutes before delegates take their seats, the interpreting booths at Koe Interpreters begin their sound check. In the quiet hall, an interpreter slips on a headset while the venue's audiovisual technician stands outside the booth door with a cable tester and an audio monitoring console. Over the next thirty minutes, they do not merely verify that sound passes from the lectern microphone into the booth earpieces; they calibrate the acoustic working environment upon which the entire meeting depends.

Simultaneous interpreting requires extraordinary auditory precision. An interpreter does not listen to a presentation the way a casual audience member does. In the booth, we must perceive every consonant, unpick rapid technical jargon, identify foreign accents, and register quiet hesitations, all while speaking continuously into our own console microphone. If the incoming audio is muffled, clipped, or contaminated with background hum, the interpreter's brain must expend enormous cognitive effort simply reconstructing missing phonemes. Within an hour, auditory fatigue sets in, concentration falters, and translation clarity degrades.

The sound check resolves these physical hazards before the meeting opens. Our interpreters work systematically with the technician through a standard acoustic checklist. First, we test direct microphone feeds from every podium, panel table, and roving handheld unit. We ensure that volume levels are balanced across all channels so the interpreter is not startled by sudden volume jumps when the floor moves from a soft-spoken chair to an energetic panelist. Second, we verify the frequency response, adjusting equalizer settings to eliminate muddy bass resonance and attenuate piercing high frequencies that cause ear fatigue over a 6.5-hour day.

Equally vital is the check of the outbound transmission. We verify that each booth's console connects cleanly to the delegate receiver system. The technician walks the hall with a wireless receiver and earpiece, confirming that the English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, French, or German channels are broadcasting on their assigned frequencies without cross-talk or static. We also verify the operation of the cough button and mute switches, ensuring that booth colleagues can confer or cough without broadcasting extraneous noise to delegates.

When a conference involves three languages and uses an English relay, the 08:15 sound check takes on an added layer of importance. In a relay setup, the Japanese or German booth listens directly to the English booth's rendition to translate speeches into their target language. The acoustic link between the two booths must be pristine. A minor delay, impedance mismatch, or signal hum in the relay feed will compound across both booths, compromising the experience of everyone in the room.

By 08:45, the sound check is complete. The technician secures the cable runs, the consoles are locked to verified levels, and our two interpreters per booth sit down with their glossary notes to review the morning agenda. When the opening gavel strikes at 09:00, the audience will hear a calm, effortless voice in their earpieces. They will rarely consider the thirty minutes of technical calibration that made such effortless listening possible.

posts.title: Consecutive notes, explained
posts.excerpt: How structured symbols and vertical margins capture meaning and emphasis during unamplified bilateral talks.
posts.content:
Consecutive interpreters do not write down words. They write down ideas: arrows for cause and result, circles for topics, a line for a change of speaker.

The page is divided by a vertical margin so that links between ideas stay visible. When the speaker pauses, the interpreter reads the page like a map and speaks it back in the other language.

It is a small-room method: bilateral talks, site visits and dinners, where a booth would be out of place.

posts.title: Two days, one board: an EN ⇄ JA meeting
posts.excerpt: A shipping group held a two-day board meeting in English and Japanese; the team was briefed a week ahead.
posts.content:
A shipping group asked for a two-day board meeting in English and Japanese. The documents arrived five working days before, and the glossary was shared two days before the meeting.

On the day the two interpreters alternated every thirty minutes. The resting colleague kept the figures and names. The chief interpreter filed the glossary notes within two business days.

posts.title: Three languages through one relay: a medical symposium
posts.excerpt: A medical-device association needed three languages in one hall; the third booth worked through English relay.
posts.content:
A medical-device association held a symposium in Chinese, English and German. We added a booth and worked through English relay.

Terminology was the main work: the speakers sent their slides early, and the interpreters built one shared glossary for all three booths.

posts.content:
